title: The Scientific Method in the Science of Machine Learning
venue: ICLR 2019 Debugging Machine Learning Models Workshop
extended_summary:
This position paper argues that contemporary machine learning research often lacks two core elements of the scientific method: explicit hypothesis formulation/testing and careful statistical treatment of uncertainty. The authors motivate the paper by pointing to reproducibility concerns, inconsistent performance across replications, and the tendency for published ML results to emphasize performance claims without adequately quantifying variation or confounding factors.

The paper does not study an educational intervention or a learner population. Instead, it proposes methodological guidance for the ML research community, drawing analogies from experimental high-energy physics. The authors describe how physics uses null and alternative hypotheses, nuisance parameters, likelihood-based estimation, and pre-registration/registered reports to support rigorous inference, and they suggest similar practices for ML experiments.

The context is research practice in machine learning rather than a school or classroom setting. The main conclusion is that ML researchers should move beyond exploratory “it works” demonstrations toward controlled, reproducible experiments with pre-specified hypotheses and explicit statistical/systematic uncertainty accounting. The paper recommends broader adoption of registered reports, negative-result publication, and closer attention to robustness and variability in claims of state-of-the-art performance.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed position paper, not an empirical study. It provides conceptual arguments and recommendations about scientific rigor in machine learning, but it does not test an intervention, compare groups, or report study methods/results relevant to K-12 outcomes.
impact_tier_rationale: There is no direct educational intervention or measured student outcome in the paper, so there is no demonstrated impact on K-12 learners, teachers, or schools. Any relevance to science education is only indirect and theoretical.
